name: Swing
question: Does the structure support another move?
intro: After the first expansion, read the range, the selling, and the demand that remains.

lessons.title: Price structure
lessons.question: What keeps repeating on the chart?
lessons.definition: Structure is the sequence of highs, lows, ranges, and reactions built over time.
lessons.why: Repeated reactions give you areas to investigate; one candle rarely tells the whole story.
checks: Several highs and lows on the same timeframe
Repeated reaction areas
Whether price holds or rejects a new range
lessons.healthy: Repeated tests and reactions support a clear working structure.
lessons.dangerous: A single bounce or wick becomes the entire thesis.
lessons.mistake: Drawing precise lines without checking the reactions behind them.
lessons.takeaway: Read repeated behavior before naming a pattern.
example: Price makes a high, pulls back, then makes a higher high.
The next pullback holds above the earlier low.
That supports rising structure; losing that low would weaken it.
evidence: Find an exact token and review observed history. Use Inspect's 5D view or an external chart for detailed candle reactions.
lessons.deeper: Old entry areas can influence later selling, but a chart cannot identify trapped holders or their motives. Structure is observed price behavior; the ownership explanation needs separate evidence.

lessons.title: Base & repricing
lessons.question: Did price visit a new range, or start living there?
lessons.definition: A base repeatedly meets selling with buying. Repricing means trading persists around a different valuation range.
lessons.why: A fast pump and an accepted new range can look similar at first.
checks: Time and repeated tests within the new range
Response to selling
Liquidity stability and coverage
lessons.healthy: The new range survives several tests with continuing activity.
lessons.dangerous: Price briefly spikes higher, then returns to the old range.
example: An illustrative MC range begins at $250k–$300k.
After expansion, trading repeatedly holds around $450k–$550k.
That supports a new base hypothesis; one touch would not.
evidence: Compare observed persistence and liquidity, then inspect candle history. Estimated MC assumes the reported supply relationship remains valid.
lessons.deeper: There is no universal number of tests or duration that certifies acceptance. State your timeframe and evidence, then identify what would disprove the new-base hypothesis.

lessons.title: Supply zones
lessons.question: Where does meaningful selling keep appearing?
lessons.definition: A supply zone is an area where observed or suspected inventory may meet returning buyers.
lessons.why: Old highs can attract profit-taking or breakeven selling, but that explanation still needs evidence.
checks: Repeated rejection near the same area
Sell sizes and surrounding activity
External history for suspected holder entries
lessons.healthy: The zone is treated as a hypothesis and tested against fresh reactions.
lessons.dangerous: A drawn rectangle is assumed to reveal exact sellers and inventory.
lessons.mistake: Treating resistance as geometry without investigating the selling.
lessons.takeaway: Look for supply behind the repeated rejection.
example: A token previously reached $1M MC, then fell to $400k.
Selling repeatedly appears as it revisits $900k–$1M.
That is a supply-zone lead; trapped-holder identity remains unproven.
evidence: Compare observed sells with estimated MC tiers. These tiers summarize activity; they do not identify holder cost basis or a guaranteed resistance zone.
lessons.deeper: Reported MC tiers depend on the price-to-supply estimate. Different pools, missing swaps, or changing supply can limit the comparison. Wallet inventory and entry levels need independent history.

lessons.title: Demand & absorption
lessons.question: How does price handle repeated selling?
lessons.definition: Absorption describes selling repeatedly meeting enough buying to limit or recover the price decline.
lessons.why: The response to selling can be more informative than the color of the last candle.
checks: Comparable sell sizes and time windows
Downside and recovery after each sell
Changes in liquidity and surrounding buys
lessons.healthy: Repeated sells meet recovery without losing the observed base.
lessons.dangerous: One support buyer props up price while broader demand weakens.
lessons.mistake: Calling smaller downside proof of absorption without checking liquidity.
lessons.takeaway: Compare the sell, the reaction, and the recovery.
example: Three illustrative $10k sells coincide with drops of 20%, 7%, then 2%.
Later declines are smaller, but pool depth also changed.
Improved absorption is one explanation; deeper liquidity is another.
evidence: Review sell sizes, nearby buys, and price history. Candles and returned swaps have separate coverage; buyer independence is not verified.
lessons.deeper: Equal dollar sells are not identical tests if pool liquidity, routing, timing, or surrounding demand changed. Compare those conditions before interpreting reduced price damage as stronger demand.

lessons.title: Holder rotation
lessons.question: Did ownership change, or only the addresses?
lessons.definition: Holder rotation transfers inventory from one group of owners to another.
lessons.why: A similar-looking chart can sit above a very different ownership structure.
checks: Actual sales versus wallet transfers
Old and new related-wallet balances
Known entry costs and missing history
lessons.healthy: Independent ownership changes are supported by traceable transactions.
lessons.dangerous: One actor splits inventory and concentration appears to improve.
lessons.mistake: Assuming lower top-holder percentages mean stronger holders.
example: Top-10 concentration falls from 40% to 25%.
Several fresh wallets received transfers from those holders.
The percentage changed; independent ownership is still unknown.
evidence: Use provider-reported holder count and concentration as leads. Trace actual ownership, entries, and transfers externally.
lessons.deeper: New holders are not automatically stronger or less likely to sell. Labels, higher estimated cost basis, and lower concentration each need supporting history, and none guarantees future behavior.

lessons.title: Expansion & pullback
lessons.question: Is the decline testing the base or breaking it?
lessons.definition: Expansion moves out of a range. A pullback tests what buying remains after that move.
lessons.why: The percentage decline alone cannot distinguish a retest from structural failure.
checks: The prior breakout area and base
Sell activity and subsequent recovery
Liquidity changes and external holder evidence
lessons.healthy: Selling cools and repeated buying stabilizes price near the prior area.
lessons.dangerous: The base fails, rebounds weaken, and liquidity deteriorates.
lessons.mistake: Calling every 30–50% drop either healthy or dead.
lessons.takeaway: Judge what the pullback does to the structure.
example: Price expands from a range, then declines 35%.
The prior breakout area holds through repeated tests.
The decline may be a retest; a sustained loss of that area weakens the view.
evidence: Use available historical candles for ranges and returned swaps for observed flow. Candle volume does not provide a buy/sell split.
lessons.deeper: Base → expansion → pullback → continuation is one possible path. Specify what would count as a failed retest before interpreting every rebound as confirmation.

lessons.title: Continuation vs distribution
lessons.question: Is buying moving price, or feeding sellers?
lessons.definition: A pause can retain demand for another move, or let existing holders sell into incoming buyers.
lessons.why: Both paths can look like sideways consolidation.
checks: Buying effort versus price progress
Repeated selling and liquidity changes
External evidence of large-holder reductions
lessons.healthy: Selling is absorbed, the range holds, and price responds to renewed demand.
lessons.dangerous: Large buying meets repeated selling with little sustained progress.
lessons.takeaway: Ask what the buying effort achieved.
example: Observed buy value increases across comparable windows.
Price repeatedly fails at the same area while large sells continue.
Investigate supply pressure; the sample alone cannot identify distributors.
evidence: Compare flow intervals, sizes, and price response. Net observed flow is not a complete market tape or proof of distribution.
lessons.deeper: Strong movement on small buying can also reflect fragile liquidity. Weak movement on heavy buying can reflect deeper liquidity or activity elsewhere. Effort versus result is a question to investigate, not a deterministic formula.

lessons.title: Swing lifecycle
lessons.question: Which part of the move are you investigating?
lessons.definition: A lifecycle is a working map: discovery, expansion, supply transfer, repricing, then a base or failure.
lessons.why: The same pause can mean different things before and after major supply transfer.
checks: What happened before the current range
Evidence of demand and ownership changes
Conditions that would support or invalidate continuation
lessons.healthy: The stage description changes when the evidence changes.
lessons.dangerous: Every token is forced into a fixed sequence or promised next stage.
lessons.mistake: Using the same interpretation at every stage.
lessons.takeaway: Locate the stage. Keep the next outcome conditional.
example: Expansion is followed by selling and a lower stable range.
Demand later returns and the range starts being tested from above.
Continuation is a hypothesis to test, not a scheduled next step.
evidence: Compare Hours and Days research context, then investigate in Inspect. Rankings do not assign verified lifecycle stages or predict returns.
lessons.deeper: Continuation and failure are branches, not compulsory destinations. If history, ownership, or current demand is missing, describe the stage as uncertain and record what evidence you need next.
